content:
Touma noticed the headache first. It was already blooming behind his eyes.

That was the first warning.

The second followed a moment later: the lights in the old transit station were too sharp. Everything seemed to have extra edges. The vending machine’s hum scraped against his teeth.

He kept moving.

Trouble outside his skull could usually be outrun. Trouble inside it tended to come along.

Near a service gate, a man in a gray coat had his hand around a boy’s wrist. The boy was a small-built teenager with a school bag hanging from one shoulder. The man held him with the bored assurance of someone following a procedure. His other hand was inside his coat.

People passed them. A few looked, then found somewhere else to look.

The boy wasn’t struggling. He stared at the man with a blank terror that seemed to have emptied him of everything, including the idea of pulling away.

Touma stopped.

It was not gallantry. It was recognition.

He was tired. His head hurt. He had no desire to find out what the man was keeping inside his coat.

There were six steps between them.

Touma took them.

“Hey.”

The man turned his head without loosening his grip.

And Touma caught the thought.

*Keep moving. Keep the kid quiet. Finish the handoff.*

Not words spoken aloud. Not even words meant for him. Just an intention, close enough and clear enough to touch.

Touma put something like a paperknife to the edge of the thought.

Then he unthought it.

For an instant, it felt as though he had pushed a pin through the inside of the world.

The man’s hand opened.

He looked down at his empty fingers. Whatever had been carrying him forward was gone, and his body seemed to discover, all at once, that it had a private appointment with gravity. He stumbled against the gate.

The boy pulled his wrist to his chest.

For half a second, Touma felt relief.

Then the second half arrived.

His memory hiccupped.

The boy looked at him. Touma looked back, waiting for something that had been there a moment ago.

There was the school bag. The frightened face. The wrist the man had held.

But the familiarity was gone.

He could feel the absence without knowing what belonged in it.

Around them, the station continued: footsteps, sharp lights, the vending machine’s hum.

It had happened with a clean, quiet cruelty.
